passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel chemotherapeutic agent on human breast cancer cell lines over a 72‑hour period. Cells were plated at a density of 1×10^5 cells per well and treated with a drug whose concentration in the medium was increased stepwise over the experiment (0, 15, 25, and 35 µM at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours, respectively). Viability was assessed using a resazurin reduction assay at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours. The following table summarizes the drug concentration and mean cell viability (% of untreated control) for each time point. Viability decreased as exposure time and drug concentration rose together, with the lowest viability observed at 72 hours. The study aims to determine the optimal dosing schedule and to explore the underlying mechanism of action via downstream signaling assays.
stem: Which time point shows the highest cell viability?
explanation: At 0 hours the drug has not yet exerted any effect, so viability is 100%. All subsequent time points show reduced viability.
trap: Choosing the 72-hour point as if longer exposure raised viability, when viability falls as drug exposure rises.

stem: In this experiment, drug concentration and exposure time increased together. Which modification would best isolate the effect of drug concentration on cell viability?

options.A: Add more time points (e.g., 96 and 120 hours) while continuing the stepwise increase in concentration
options.B: Treat separate wells with 0, 15, 25, or 35 µM held constant throughout, and measure viability in all wells at the same time point
options.C: Increase the plating density to 2×10^5 cells per well
options.D: Measure viability with a second assay in addition to resazurin reduction

explanation: Correct: B. Holding each concentration constant in parallel wells and measuring all wells at one time point removes exposure time as a variable, so differences in viability reflect concentration alone (a true dose–response curve). Why the others are wrong: A) Extra time points keep concentration and time rising together, so the confound remains. C) Changing cell density alters growth conditions but does not separate concentration from time. D) A second assay may improve measurement validity but leaves concentration and time confounded.
trap: Choosing to add time points under the same stepwise schedule, which collects more data but still changes concentration and time together.

stem: What is the mean of the drug concentrations listed for the 24-hour and 48-hour time points?
explanation: Correct: (15 + 25) / 2 = 20 µM. Why the others are wrong: A) 10 µM is not the mean of 15 and 25 µM. B) 15 µM is only the 24-hour concentration. D) 25 µM is only the 48-hour concentration.
trap: Picking the 48-hour value (25 µM) instead of averaging the two listed concentrations.

stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the data?

options.A: Viability fell at each successive time point as drug concentration rose.
options.C: The drug concentration at 48 hours is 25 µM.
options.D: Viability at 0 hours is 85% of the untreated control.

explanation: Correct: At 0 hours no drug has been applied, so viability is 100% of the untreated control; 85% is the 24-hour value. Why the others are wrong: A) viability went 100, 85, 70 and 55% as time and concentration rose together. B) 55% at 72 hours is the lowest value in the table. C) the table lists 25 µM at 48 hours.
trap: Confusing the 24-hour viability (85%) with the 0-hour baseline of 100%.

stem: The data most directly support which of the following concepts?
explanation: The passage reports changes in cell viability in response to drug concentration and time, illustrating the drug’s pharmacodynamic effect on target cells.
trap: Students may incorrectly select pharmacokinetics, but the data describe effect rather than drug disposition.
